    RING (C ≈ 0)
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  
    Star: all betweenness concentrated in the hub.
    Ring: every node has identical centrality — no decapitation target.
  









TipIntelligence Application: Al-Qaeda Network Transformation



Everton’s analysis of Al-Qaeda’s organizational structure captures the centralization dynamic across an actual disruption campaign:
Pre-2001 — Al-Qaeda showed high betweenness centralization: a small number of senior brokers (notably Bin Laden’s lieutenants in Afghanistan) routed communication and coordination between cells across multiple continents. This made decapitation a viable strategic option, and the 2001–2002 campaign in Afghanistan successfully removed or disrupted several of these high-betweenness nodes.
Post-2003 reorganization — Surviving affiliates deliberately flattened the network structure. Regional affiliates (AQI, AQAP, AQIM) operated with substantially more autonomy. Betweenness centralization dropped significantly. Decapitation of individual nodes became less effective; the network had evolved to make itself more resilient to precisely the strategy that had worked against it.3
Analytical implication: Compute centralization at the start of any sustained disruption campaign. If centralization is declining across time-series analysis, the network is adapting to targeting. Shift strategy accordingly.

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Degree Centrality
Degree centrality is the simplest and computationally cheapest centrality measure. It captures local connectivity — how active a node is in terms of direct ties — but says nothing about the node’s position in the broader network structure.



Undirected Degree Centrality
\[C_D(v) = \deg(v)\]
Normalized (allows comparison across networks of different sizes):
\[C_D^*(v) = \frac{\deg(v)}{n - 1}\]
where \(n - 1\) is the maximum possible degree in a simple graph on \(n\) nodes. A value of 1.0 means the node is connected to every other node; 0 means isolated.


Directed Degree Centrality
In directed networks, degree splits into two analytically distinct measures:

In-degree centrality \(C_D^-(v) = \frac{\deg^-(v)}{n-1}\): measures prestige or popularity — how many others direct ties toward this node. High in-degree suggests authority, leadership, or target-of-information status.
Out-degree centrality \(C_D^+(v) = \frac{\deg^+(v)}{n-1}\): measures activity or initiative — how many outgoing connections this node initiates. High out-degree suggests recruiters, propagandists, financiers, or coordinators.



Strength Centrality (Weighted Networks)
When edge weights encode relationship intensity (call frequency, transaction volume, message count), raw degree undercounts activity:
\[C_S(v) = \sum_{u \in N(v)} w(v, u)\]
A node that calls one contact 200 times may be more operationally significant than one with 10 contacts called once each. Strength centrality captures this; degree does not.








WarningWhen Degree Centrality Is Misleading



In compartmentalized dark networks, operational leaders deliberately minimize their degree to reduce exposure risk. They are not the most socially active actors — they are the most carefully connected ones.
Who tends to have high degree in such networks: - Logistics coordinators and couriers (must contact many parties) - Safe house operators (multiple visitors) - Social facilitators and recruiters (broad contact base)
Who tends to have low degree despite high authority: - Cell leaders (contacts only a small number of trusted subordinates and one superior) - Financiers (contact through cutouts) - Planners (isolated from operational layer)
Degree centrality in these networks systematically identifies the support layer, not the command layer. In the Jemaah Islamiyah network analyzed by Everton, the most degree-central actors were largely logistical; operational planners ranked mid-to-low on degree but high on betweenness.4

title: Centrality and Influence
section: H-Index and Coreness as Degree Alternatives
text:
H-Index and Coreness as Degree Alternatives
Two alternatives to raw degree provide more nuanced pictures of local embedding:
H-index (adapted from citation analysis): Node \(v\) has h-index \(h\) if it has at least \(h\) neighbors each of which has degree \(\geq h\), and no larger \(h\) satisfies this condition. H-index rewards having well-connected neighbors, not just many neighbors — a node with 5 neighbors each of degree \(\geq 5\) has h-index 5, while a node with 10 neighbors each of degree 1 has h-index 1.
Coreness (from \(k\)-core decomposition, covered in Week 3): the coreness of a node equals the largest \(k\)-core it belongs to. Unlike degree, coreness captures the density of the node’s neighborhood recursively — a node with high coreness is embedded in a mutually dense subgraph, not merely attached to many peripheral actors.
Both measures are computable in \(O(m)\) and available in NetworkX (nx.core_number(G)) and Gephi. They are particularly useful as supplements to degree when screening for inner-circle membership in dark networks.

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Closeness Centrality
Closeness centrality measures how efficiently a node can reach all others — a proxy for information dissemination speed and early warning sensitivity.



Definition
\[C_C(v) = \frac{n-1}{\sum_{u \neq v} d(v, u)}\]
The numerator normalizes the measure so that a star center (the single node optimally placed to reach all others in one step) receives a score of 1.0. Low closeness means the node is peripheral — far from the network’s informational core.


Connected Graph Variants
The standard formula is undefined when the graph is disconnected (the denominator includes \(d(v,u) = \infty\) for unreachable nodes). Two approaches:

Wasserman-Faust variant: compute closeness only over reachable nodes, then normalize by the proportion of nodes reachable: \(C_C^{WF}(v) = \frac{n_r - 1}{n - 1} \cdot \frac{n_r - 1}{\sum_{u \in R(v)} d(v,u)}\), where \(n_r = |R(v)|\).
Harmonic centrality: sum the reciprocals of all distances, setting \(1/\infty = 0\) by convention:5

\[C_H(v) = \sum_{u \neq v} \frac{1}{d(v, u)}\]
Harmonic centrality is the preferred choice for intelligence network data, which almost always produces disconnected graphs due to collection incompleteness.


Intelligence Applications

Identify nodes best positioned for rapid information dissemination (highest closeness = fastest broadcast reach)
Identify nodes that would detect threats earliest in a monitoring network (peripheral nodes learn last)
Locate early warning sensors: an analyst wanting to monitor a network with limited collection resources should target high-closeness nodes to maximize the fraction of network activity observed

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Betweenness Centrality
Betweenness centrality measures how often a node lies on the shortest path between other pairs of nodes. A node with high betweenness controls information flow, can act as a broker or gatekeeper, and represents a structural chokepoint.



Definition
\[C_B(v) = \sum_{\substack{s \neq v \neq t \\ s < t}} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}}\]
where:

\(\sigma_{st}\) = total number of shortest paths from \(s\) to \(t\)
\(\sigma_{st}(v)\) = number of those shortest paths that pass through \(v\) as an intermediate node
The ratio \(\sigma_{st}(v)/\sigma_{st}\) is the fraction of geodesics from \(s\) to \(t\) that go through \(v\)
Summed over all unordered pairs not including \(v\)

Normalized (divide by the number of possible pairs): for undirected graphs, divide by \(\binom{n-1}{2} = \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}\).


What Betweenness Captures

Brokerage: control over information flowing between otherwise disconnected parts of the network
Gatekeeping: ability to filter, delay, modify, or distort messages passing through
Structural hole occupancy: nodes bridging gaps between clusters (Burt’s structural holes, Week 3)6
Targeted disruption value: removing a high-betweenness node fragments the network far more efficiently than removing a high-degree node in compartmentalized networks



Edge Betweenness
\[C_B(e) = \sum_{s \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(e)}{\sigma_{st}}\]
Edges with high betweenness carry disproportionate network traffic. Severing a high-betweenness edge can fragment the network into disconnected components without requiring the removal of any actor — potentially less detectable operationally.


Computational Complexity
Computed via the Brandes algorithm: \(O(nm)\) for unweighted graphs; \(O(nm + n^2 \log n)\) for weighted. For very large networks (\(n > 10^5\)), approximation algorithms are available. Gephi and NetworkX implement Brandes exactly for intelligence-scale networks (typically \(n < 10^4\)).








WarningThe Betweenness-Targeting Rule



For network disruption in compartmentalized dark networks: target nodes with the highest betweenness, not highest degree.
Betweenness identifies the coordinators and cutouts who route communication across otherwise separate cells — the structural chokepoints. Removing them severs inter-cell pathways even when the cells themselves remain intact.
In flat, redundant networks where many alternative geodesics exist, betweenness becomes less useful as a targeting signal. In those cases, community-level analysis and edge removal may be more effective.








NoteComputational Note



Betweenness is the most computationally expensive of the standard centrality measures at \(O(nm)\), compared to \(O(n + m)\) for degree. For a network with \(n=1{,}000\) nodes and \(m=5{,}000\) edges, Brandes runs in milliseconds on modern hardware. For \(n=100{,}000\), approximate algorithms are recommended. NetworkX defaults to the exact Brandes implementation.








TipKey Insight: Low Degree ≠ Low Betweenness



In the conceptual example above, Node D has degree 2 (the minimum for a non-isolated, non-leaf node on any meaningful path) but maximum betweenness (every path between the two clusters passes through D). This is the archetypal dark network broker profile: minimally connected, maximally controlling.

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Eigenvector Centrality
Degree centrality treats all neighbors equally — a tie to a well-connected hub counts the same as a tie to an isolated peripheral node. Eigenvector centrality corrects this by making each node’s score proportional to the sum of its neighbors’ scores, evaluated recursively.



Definition
\[C_E(v) = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{u \in N(v)} C_E(u)\]
In matrix form: \(A \mathbf{C}_E = \lambda \mathbf{C}_E\)
The centrality vector \(\mathbf{C}_E\) is an eigenvector of the adjacency matrix \(A\), and \(\lambda\) is the corresponding eigenvalue. The Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees that for connected graphs, the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) has all positive entries — this is the eigenvector centrality vector.7


Power Iteration (Convergence)
In practice, computed iteratively:

Initialize all nodes with score 1
For each node, replace its score with the sum of its neighbors’ current scores
Normalize the score vector to prevent divergence
Repeat until scores stabilize (convergence criterion: \(\|\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} - \mathbf{x}^{(t)}\| < \epsilon\))

WarningLimitation: Disconnected Graphs and Directed Networks



Eigenvector centrality has important failure modes:

Disconnected graphs: nodes in isolated components receive score 0 even if they are central within their component. The largest eigenvector has zero entries for unreachable nodes.
Directed graphs with sinks: a node that receives edges from high-scoring nodes but has no outgoing edges concentrates score without distributing it. Eventually all score drains into sink components.

Katz centrality and PageRank both address these problems through different mechanisms (see below).








TipIntelligence Application: Arms Broker Networks



In a network linking arms brokers, suppliers, end-users, and financial intermediaries, eigenvector centrality identifies actors who are connected to the most important other actors — not merely the most active ones.
A mid-level broker who has moderate degree but connects directly to major state-level suppliers and NATO-sanctioned end-users will score high on eigenvector centrality. This profile — moderate activity, elite connections — is characteristic of senior facilitators who deliberately minimize their transaction footprint while maintaining access to the network’s core.
Contrast with degree centrality: low-level couriers and logistics coordinators will often have higher degree but lower eigenvector scores, correctly deprioritizing them relative to the facilitator.

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Katz Centrality
Katz centrality addresses eigenvector centrality’s failures on directed graphs and disconnected networks by adding a baseline score \(\beta > 0\) to every node regardless of incoming connections:
\[C_K(v) = \alpha \sum_{u} A_{uv} C_K(u) + \beta\]
In matrix form: \(\mathbf{C}_K = \beta(I - \alpha A^\top)^{-1} \mathbf{1}\)

\(\alpha\) (attenuation factor): \(0 < \alpha < 1/\lambda_1\). Longer paths contribute exponentially less — indirect influence decays with path length. Setting \(\alpha \to 0\) collapses Katz to a constant; setting \(\alpha \to 1/\lambda_1\) approximates eigenvector centrality.
\(\beta\): the baseline score ensuring no node receives zero centrality due to structural isolation. Typically set to 1.

Katz centrality is interpretable as a weighted count of all walks from all other nodes to \(v\), with walks of length \(k\) penalized by \(\alpha^k\). This makes it a measure of how reachable a node is along paths of all lengths, with shorter paths weighted more heavily.8

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
PageRank
PageRank, developed by Brin and Page for web link analysis, is a damped version of eigenvector centrality designed for directed graphs with disconnected components:
\[PR(v) = \frac{1-d}{n} + d \sum_{u \in \text{in}(v)} \frac{PR(u)}{\deg^+(u)}\]
where \(d \approx 0.85\) is the damping factor — the probability that a random walker follows an outgoing link rather than teleporting to a random node.

Each node distributes its PageRank equally among all its out-neighbors
The \((1-d)/n\) term prevents score from concentrating in sink nodes (nodes with no outgoing edges) via random teleportation
Handles disconnected directed graphs naturally
Converges via power iteration to a unique stationary distribution







NoteIntelligence Application: Influence Operations and Information Networks



In a retweet network, nodes are accounts and directed edges represent retweet relationships (A retweets B → B’s content reaches A’s followers). PageRank on this network identifies accounts whose content propagates most widely — not just accounts with many followers (degree), but accounts whose content is amplified by other high-PageRank accounts.
A coordinated influence operation may use a collection of low-follower sock puppet accounts (hub layer) to drive amplification of a small number of high-credibility accounts (authority layer). PageRank of the high-credibility accounts rises because they receive links from many accounts that themselves receive links from others.
In practice: Graphika, DFRLab, and Stanford Internet Observatory have all used eigenvector-family centrality measures (including PageRank variants) as signals in influence operation attribution work.9

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
HITS: Hubs and Authorities
HITS (Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search), developed by Kleinberg, decomposes centrality into two mutually reinforcing scores — a more nuanced decomposition than PageRank’s single score.10



Algorithm
Authority score \(x(v)\): a node is a good authority if it is pointed to by good hubs.
\[x(v) = \sum_{u \,:\, (u,v) \in E} y(u)\]
Hub score \(y(v)\): a node is a good hub if it points to many good authorities.
\[y(v) = \sum_{u \,:\, (v,u) \in E} x(u)\]
The two equations are mutually recursive: authorities gain score from hubs pointing to them; hubs gain score from the authorities they point to. Computed iteratively until convergence.
Matrix form: Authority vector \(\mathbf{x}\) is the principal eigenvector of \(A^\top A\); hub vector \(\mathbf{y}\) is the principal eigenvector of \(A A^\top\).


HITS vs. PageRank

PageRank: single score per node; more incoming links from high-scoring nodes = higher rank
HITS: two-dimensional; a node can score high as a hub without being an authority (a news aggregator pointing to many sources), or high as an authority without being a hub (a primary source rarely linking out)
Disruption implication: the two roles typically belong to different actors; targeting strategies differ accordingly

TipExtremist Network Application



In an online extremist content network:

Authorities: accounts that produce original ideological content widely reshared — the ideological producers. Disrupting authorities degrades the quality and volume of content supply.
Hubs: accounts that aggregate and amplify content from many authorities, often adding minimal original material — the amplification layer. Disrupting hubs degrades reach and exposure.

The two roles frequently belong to different actors with different operational profiles. HITS identifies both simultaneously; PageRank would conflate them.

section: Comparing Centrality Measures: A Decision Framework

Comparing Centrality Measures: A Decision Framework
Centrality Measure Selection Guide








Measure

Primary Intelligence Use




Degree

Social hubs, recruitment leads, logistics nodes


In-degree

Leadership identification, information flow targets


Out-degree

Recruiters, financiers, propagandists


Strength

Closeness
Who can reach others fastest?

Betweenness
Who controls information flow?
Coordinators, cutouts, brokers; disruption targeting


Eigenvector
Who is connected to important actors?
Elite network membership, prestige identification


PageRank
Who receives from high-scoring senders?

HITS Hub

Amplifiers in information networks


HITS Authority
Who is cited by many hubs?

When Measures Disagree
Disagreement among centrality measures is analytically informative, not a problem to be resolved by picking one measure. Each disagreement pattern carries a structural signature:

High betweenness + low degree — classic cutout or broker profile; bridges clusters with minimal direct exposure; high disruption value
High degree + low betweenness — local hub within a dense cluster; active but not a bridge; resilient to removal (neighbors remain connected to each other via alternative paths)
High eigenvector + low betweenness — well-embedded in a high-status elite cluster but not a structural bridge; removal degrades prestige without fragmenting the network
High closeness + low betweenness — centrally located but not a unique pathway; removal does not fragment but increases average path length

Best practice: compute and present all major centrality measures as a ranked table alongside node attributes. Agreement across measures increases confidence in structural importance; disagreement signals a node worth deeper examination.11

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Centrality Under Incomplete Data
All intelligence network data is incomplete. Missing nodes and edges systematically distort centrality scores, and the distortion is not uniform across measures.12



Sensitivity Patterns by Measure
Degree centrality — relatively robust to missing edges. If missing data are roughly random and representative, degree rank order is approximately preserved. Fails when collection is systematically biased toward certain node types (e.g., focusing collection on known associates of a small set of seed nodes, inflating their degree artificially).
Betweenness centrality — highly sensitive to missing nodes and edges. A single missing bridge node can radically alter all betweenness scores in the rest of the graph. If the highest-betweenness actor is not yet identified in collection, the second highest-betweenness actor will appear falsely prominent. Betweenness rankings should always be caveated for potential collection gaps.
Closeness centrality — fails or gives misleading results under high incompleteness. Especially problematic in disconnected graphs (collection artifacts produce apparent disconnection that inflates peripheral scores). Use harmonic closeness and report with explicit data completeness flags.
Eigenvector / PageRank — moderately sensitive. Robust if missing data are random; fragile if missing data are systematic. If collection under-samples high-degree nodes (e.g., encrypted messaging platforms reduce visibility of high-volume communicators), eigenvector centrality systematically underestimates scores of adjacent nodes.



Mitigation Strategies

Sensitivity analysis: compute centrality after randomly adding or removing 10–20% of edges; observe rank stability. If the top-3 ranking is invariant, findings are moderately robust.
Multiple imputation: estimate likely missing edges from attribute similarity, shared affiliations, or network structural models (exponential random graph models); compute centrality on multiple imputed networks; report the distribution of rank scores.
Confidence-weighted networks: assign lower edge weights to lower-confidence source reports; compute weighted centrality. This degrades the influence of poorly-sourced ties without removing them entirely.
Qualitative validation: triangulate centrality findings against HUMINT or SIGINT characterizations of node roles. If betweenness analysis identifies Node X as a coordinator and independent source reporting describes X as a logistics driver, the discrepancy warrants deeper examination of both the data and the analysis.







WarningRequired Caveat Language



Centrality findings in intelligence products must be accompanied by a data completeness assessment. Model language:
“Node X ranks highest on normalized betweenness centrality (\(C_B^* = 0.42\)) in the reconstructed network. This ranking is based on [N] confirmed relationships from [source types]. Betweenness centrality is highly sensitive to missing bridge nodes; collection gaps in [specific domain or time period] may significantly alter this ranking. Sensitivity analysis across 100 random 15% edge deletions shows rank-1 stability in 73% of trials.”

Five Network Disruption Strategies
The appropriate disruption strategy depends on the network’s structural properties — particularly its centralization, density, and degree distribution.

Decapitation — remove highest-betweenness nodes (coordinators and bridges). Most effective in hierarchical, centralized networks. Least effective in flat, distributed networks where multiple alternative paths exist.
Hub removal — remove highest-degree nodes. Most effective in scale-free networks where hubs are rare (power-law degree distribution). Random node removal is ineffective in scale-free networks; targeted hub removal causes rapid collapse.
Edge removal — sever highest-betweenness edges (bridges between clusters). Splits the network into disconnected components without removing actors who may reconstitute links or resurface through other nodes. May be less detectable than node removal.
Peripheral disruption — target low-centrality nodes (recruitment pools, financiers, logisticians). Degrades network capacity and creates friction without triggering immediate reorganization or alerting the core network.
Broker isolation — remove high-betweenness, low-degree nodes (cutouts). Disrupts covert coordination while minimizing evidence that network structure was the targeting criterion, rather than individual attribute information.







TipEmpirical Finding: Jemaah Islamiyah Disruption Simulation



Everton’s simulation analysis of the Jemaah Islamiyah (JI) network in Southeast Asia compared the effectiveness of betweenness-based versus degree-based targeting strategies:

Removing the top 10% of nodes by betweenness centrality reduced the giant component size by 43%
Removing the top 10% of nodes by degree centrality reduced the giant component size by only 19%

Betweenness-based targeting was more than twice as effective at fragmenting the network as degree-based targeting, using the same number of “actions.”
The finding generalizes: in compartmentalized dark networks that deliberately minimize hub formation (violating the scale-free assumption), betweenness-based targeting consistently outperforms degree-based targeting. In scale-free networks (more common in social media and open organizational networks), degree-based hub removal can be comparably or more effective.13

title: Centrality and Influence
section: Centrality in Practice: Gephi and NetworkX
text:
Centrality in Practice: Gephi and NetworkX



Gephi

Statistics panel: one-click computation of degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector, PageRank, and modularity (community detection)
Results stored immediately as node attributes; directly available for visual encoding
Visual encoding workflow: run statistics → open Appearance panel → map centrality attribute to node size or color gradient → export image
Export: full centrality table as CSV for reporting and integration with other tools
Limitation: treats multigraphs and self-loops inconsistently; verify graph type before running. Betweenness computation uses the Brandes algorithm but may produce unexpected results on directed graphs with unreachable nodes.



i2 Analyst Notebook

Built-in Social Network Analysis module computes degree, betweenness, and closeness
Integrated with entity attributes, timeline analysis, and link chart visualization
Output: ranked node list visualized directly on the chart
Standard tool in classified network analysis environments; compatible with US Government classification workflows
Does not natively support eigenvector, PageRank, or HITS — use NetworkX for those measures and import results




NetworkX (Python)
import networkx as nx
import pandas as pd

# Load from CSV edge list
G = nx.read_edgelist(
    'data.csv',
    delimiter=',',
    create_using=nx.DiGraph(),
    data=[('weight', float), ('type', str)]
)

# Compute all major centrality measures
results = {
    'degree':       nx.degree_centrality(G),
    'in_degree':    nx.in_degree_centrality(G),
    'out_degree':   nx.out_degree_centrality(G),
    'closeness':    nx.closeness_centrality(G),
    'betweenness':  nx.betweenness_centrality(G, normalized=True),
    'eigenvector':  nx.eigenvector_centrality(G, max_iter=1000),
    'pagerank':     nx.pagerank(G, alpha=0.85),
    'hits_hubs':    nx.hits(G)[0],
    'hits_auth':    nx.hits(G)[1],
    'coreness':     nx.core_number(G.to_undirected()),
}

# Build comparison table
df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values('betweenness', ascending=False)
print(df.round(3).to_string())

# Export
df.to_csv('centrality_results.csv')
Full programmatic control; reproducible; scales to networks with millions of nodes using approximate algorithms (nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=100) for \(k\)-sample approximation).

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Key Formulas


Degree centrality (normalized)

\(C_D^*(v) = \dfrac{\deg(v)}{n - 1}\)

In/Out-degree centrality

\(C_D^-(v) = \dfrac{\deg^-(v)}{n-1}\); \(\;\;C_D^+(v) = \dfrac{\deg^+(v)}{n-1}\)

Strength centrality

\(C_S(v) = \sum_{u \in N(v)} w(v, u)\)

Closeness centrality

\(C_C(v) = \dfrac{n-1}{\sum_{u \neq v} d(v,u)}\)

Harmonic centrality

\(C_H(v) = \sum_{u \neq v} \dfrac{1}{d(v,u)}\), with \(1/\infty = 0\)

Betweenness centrality

\(C_B(v) = \sum_{s < t,\; s,t \neq v} \dfrac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}}\)

Edge betweenness

\(C_B(e) = \sum_{s \neq t} \dfrac{\sigma_{st}(e)}{\sigma_{st}}\)

Freeman centralization index

\(C_X(G) = \dfrac{\sum_v [C_X(v^*) - C_X(v)]}{\max_{G'} \sum_v [C_X(v^*) - C_X(v)]}\)

Eigenvector centrality

\(A\,\mathbf{C}_E = \lambda_1\,\mathbf{C}_E\) (principal eigenvector of \(A\))

Katz centrality

\(\mathbf{C}_K = \beta(I - \alpha A^\top)^{-1}\mathbf{1}\), with \(\alpha < 1/\lambda_1\)

PageRank

\(PR(v) = \dfrac{1-d}{n} + d\!\!\sum_{u \in \text{in}(v)}\!\!\dfrac{PR(u)}{\deg^+(u)}\), \(d \approx 0.85\)

HITS authority

\(x(v) = \sum_{u:(u,v)\in E} y(u)\); converges to eigenvector of \(A^\top A\)

HITS hub

\(y(v) = \sum_{u:(v,u)\in E} x(u)\); converges to eigenvector of \(A\,A^\top\)

title: Centrality and Influence
text:
Key Analytical Principles

No single centrality measure is universally correct — the choice must be driven by the analytical question (communication speed → closeness; structural chokepoints → betweenness; prestige → eigenvector).
In compartmentalized dark networks, betweenness is the most valuable measure for disruption targeting; degree systematically underperforms and may misidentify support-layer actors as leadership.
Disagreement among measures is analytically informative: high betweenness / low degree = cutout profile; high eigenvector / low betweenness = embedded elite with no bridging role.
Betweenness is the measure most sensitive to data incompleteness — always caveat betweenness findings with a data completeness statement and sensitivity analysis.
Simulate disruption effects before recommending targeting: compute component count, giant component size, and average path length pre- and post-removal; rank alternative targets by disruption effect size.
Network-level centralization informs strategy selection: high centralization → decapitation is viable; low centralization → edge removal, financial disruption, or peripheral attrition may be more effective.

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
What Is a Network?






NoteFormal Definition



A network (or graph) is a set of entities (nodes/vertices) connected by relationships (edges/links). Formally: \(G = (V, E)\) where \(V\) is the vertex set and \(E \subseteq V \times V\) is the edge set.


The formalism matters because the same mathematical structure underlies any relational system. Terrorist cells, power grids, financial flows, and social media platforms all reduce to nodes and edges. Shared formalism means shared analytical tools across disparate domains, and quantitative rigor reduces analyst bias in pattern recognition.
Networks are not merely visualizations — they are structures that encode relationships. Visualization is one output; analysis is the goal.
Why this formalism matters:

The same mathematical structure underlies any relational system
Terrorist cells, power grids, financial flows, and social media all reduce to nodes and edges
Shared formalism means shared analytical tools across domains
Quantitative rigor reduces analyst bias in pattern recognition

title: What is Network Analysis?
section: A Brief History of Network Science
text:
A Brief History of Network Science
Network analysis has roots in three disciplines that converged over three centuries: mathematics, sociology, and physics. The following timeline traces the major developments from Euler’s foundational insight to the intelligence community’s adoption of social network analysis.


1736 — Euler’s Königsberg Bridge Problem

The first formal graph theory problem. Euler demonstrated that traversing all seven bridges of Königsberg without repetition was impossible, and that an Eulerian path requires every node to have even degree. This established the field of graph theory.1

1930s–1960s — Sociometry

Jacob Moreno developed sociograms — visual representations of interpersonal relationships — as a tool for mapping social structure in small groups. This was the first systematic use of network visualization in the social sciences.2

1960s — Random Graph Theory

Erdős and Rényi established probability models for graph formation, creating a mathematical foundation for understanding how connectivity emerges in large networks.3

1967 — Small World Experiment

Milgram’s chain-letter experiment demonstrated empirically that any two people in the United States were connected through an average of about six intermediaries — what became known as “six degrees of separation.”4

1998 — Small-World Networks

Watts and Strogatz formalized the clustering/path-length tradeoff that characterizes most real-world networks: high local clustering and short average path lengths — a combination that random graph models could not explain.5

1999 — Scale-Free Networks

Barabási and Albert showed that many real networks (the web, protein interaction networks, citation graphs) grow via preferential attachment, producing power-law degree distributions: a few “hub” nodes with very high degree, and many nodes with very low degree.6

2001–2002 — Intelligence Application

Following the September 11 attacks, Krebs mapped the hijacker network and demonstrated how social network analysis could reveal organizational structure, key connectors, and vulnerability points in covert cells. This brought SNA into mainstream national security discourse.7

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Core Vocabulary: Nodes and Edges

Nodes (Vertices)
Nodes represent the entities in a network. They can be persons, organizations, locations, events, documents, accounts, or states — any discrete unit that can form a relationship with another. Nodes carry attributes: demographic characteristics, role labels, capacity values, status flags, or any metadata relevant to the analytical problem. The total node count \(|V|\) is called the order of the graph.


Edges (Links, Ties)
Edges represent the relationships between nodes. They can encode communication, financial transactions, organizational membership, trust, kinship, co-occurrence in an event, or any other meaningful connection. The total edge count \(|E|\) is called the size of the graph. Like nodes, edges carry attributes — and attribute quality is a major driver of analytical quality.
Edge Attribute Examples in Intelligence Contexts



Attribute

WarningAnalyst Note



Attribute quality drives analytical quality. A network with poorly coded edge types or missing weights produces misleading centrality scores. Data quality assessment must precede structural interpretation.

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Graph Types and Directionality

By Edge Direction

Undirected: Edges have no directionality; the relationship is symmetric (e.g., co-membership in an organization). If A is connected to B, B is equally connected to A.
Directed (digraph): Edges have a source and a target; the relationship is asymmetric (e.g., wire transfers, command authority, web hyperlinks). A directing to B does not imply B directing to A.
Mixed: Some edges are directed, some are not — common when modeling systems with both symmetric and asymmetric relationship types.



By Edge Multiplicity

Simple graph: At most one edge between any pair of nodes; no self-loops. The standard graph type for most SNA applications.
Multigraph: Multiple edges allowed between the same pair of nodes (e.g., a phone call and a financial transaction between the same two actors).
Pseudograph: Self-loops permitted (e.g., a shell company transacting with itself to obscure a money trail).



By Edge Weight

Unweighted: Presence or absence only; all edges treated as equal regardless of relationship strength or frequency.
Weighted: A numeric value on each edge encodes magnitude — call frequency, transaction volume, relationship strength. Weighting changes virtually every centrality measure.



By Node Type

Unipartite (one-mode): All nodes are the same type (e.g., all persons). The most common network type in SNA.
Bipartite (two-mode): Two distinct node types; edges only run between types, never within (e.g., persons and the events they attended).8 Bipartite networks can be projected into unipartite networks at the cost of information loss.
Multipartite / Multilayer: Multiple node types or multiple relationship layers — increasingly common in complex intelligence problems.

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Network Density and Sparsity
Density \(\Delta\) measures how many edges actually exist relative to the maximum number possible:
\[\Delta = \frac{|E|}{|V|(|V|-1)/2} \quad \text{(undirected)}\]
\[\Delta = \frac{|E|}{|V|(|V|-1)} \quad \text{(directed)}\]
A \(\Delta\) of 1.0 is a complete graph (every node connected to every other); \(\Delta = 0.0\) is an empty graph. Most real-world networks — especially illicit ones — are sparse, with \(\Delta \ll 0.1\).






TipWorked Example



A network with \(|V| = 10\) nodes and \(|E| = 12\) edges (undirected):
\[\Delta = \frac{12}{10 \cdot 9 / 2} = \frac{12}{45} \approx 0.267\]
About 27% of all possible connections exist — moderately sparse. For comparison, the 9/11 hijacker network had density \(\approx 0.16\).9



Intelligence Implications of Density

Dense networks have high redundancy, strong group cohesion, and are harder to disrupt — removing any single node changes the network structure relatively little.
Sparse networks rely on key connectors (nodes with high betweenness centrality); removal of those nodes can fragment the network. Compartmentalized illicit networks are deliberately sparse for operational security.10







WarningKey Point



Density alone does not identify which connections matter — centrality measures do that. Density is a global network property; analyst targeting requires node-level structural metrics.

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Financial and Transaction Networks
Financial networks are typically bipartite or directed weighted graphs linking persons/entities to accounts and institutions. Edge weight encodes transaction volume; edge direction encodes flow. The temporal dimension is analytically critical: layering, placement, and integration in money laundering occur in sequence, and time-ordered edge data can expose the operational logic of the scheme.
Key analytical goals in financial network analysis:

Trace illicit funds across jurisdictions and shell entities
Identify structuring patterns (transactions just below reporting thresholds)
Detect anomalous flows inconsistent with declared business activity
Map financial controllers versus operational actors (often different nodes)
Identify chokepoints suitable for sanctions enforcement







NoteCase: Hawala Networks



Informal value transfer systems (hawala) operate as sparse, trust-based networks connecting brokers (hawaladars) across jurisdictions. No physical currency crosses borders — debts are settled through reciprocal book-keeping between brokers. Network analysis identifies broker communities, geographic reach, settlement patterns, and high-betweenness brokers who connect otherwise separate regional clusters.11


Key data sources: FinCEN Suspicious Activity Reports, SWIFT transaction data, corporate registry filings, beneficial ownership databases, Panama/Pandora Papers.

title: What is Network Analysis?
section: Dark Networks: Illicit and Covert Systems
text:
Dark Networks: Illicit and Covert Systems
Dark networks are clandestine, trust-based networks that operate outside legal or institutional frameworks. They include terrorist organizations, drug trafficking networks, proliferation supply chains, and criminal enterprises.12 Their structural properties differ systematically from legal organizations — and those differences are analytically exploitable.

Distinctive Properties

Operational security constraints: Actors deliberately limit connectivity to reduce exposure. The result is sparse, compartmentalized structure with few ties crossing cell boundaries.
Secrecy-efficiency tradeoff: More connected networks are more efficient operationally but more vulnerable to infiltration and decapitation.13 The optimal balance depends on the threat environment.
Trust substitutes for formal structure: Kinship, shared ethnicity, and shared criminal history replace bureaucratic coordination — relationships that are harder to disrupt than formal authority structures.
Adaptive reorganization: Networks restructure after disruption. Static analysis understates resilience; temporal analysis is required to assess how a network responds to intervention.







WarningThe Secrecy-Efficiency Tradeoff




Highly connected cells coordinate well operationally — but one arrested member can expose many others.
Highly compartmentalized cells resist infiltration — but cannot coordinate complex, multi-step operations.
Sophisticated networks modularize: dense internal clusters, sparse inter-cluster bridges.
Analytical implication: Bridge nodes (high betweenness centrality) are the highest-value targets for network disruption.









TipEmpirical Reference



Analysis of 43 terrorist networks found an average density of 0.047 — far sparser than equivalent legal organizations operating at similar scale.14

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Why Network Analysis for Intelligence?
Traditional intelligence analysis is predominantly attribute-focused: who is this person, what are their known associations, what is their role? Network analysis shifts the paradigm to relational-focused: what position does this person occupy in a structure, who do they connect, and what would change if they were removed?

What Traditional Analysis Misses

Attribute-focused analysis misses relational structure — a mid-level actor with weak individual attributes may be the critical broker between two otherwise disconnected factions
Hierarchical org charts miss informal influence and actual communication patterns
Individual-level reporting does not aggregate to systemic vulnerability assessment
Human analysts cannot hold large relational datasets in working memory; computational tools are required



What Network Analysis Adds

Structural discovery: Identifies roles not evident from individual profiles — gatekeepers, brokers, isolates, and peripheral recruiters
Comparative assessment: Compare network states over time or across cases to identify change
Targeting prioritization: Rank nodes by structural criticality, not just profile prominence or seniority
Effect prediction: Model the consequences of node or edge removal before action is taken15







NoteThe Analytical Value Proposition



Network analysis transforms intelligence from a collection of facts about entities into a model of relationships — and relationships are where power, influence, vulnerability, and intent live.


Domains where network analysis is established practice:
Social network analysis for counterterrorism cell mapping and leadership targeting; trafficking route and financial flow analysis for counternarcotics; supplier network mapping for counterproliferation; amplification network attribution for influence operations; vulnerability modeling for critical infrastructure protection; sanctions evasion and money laundering tracing for financial intelligence; threat actor infrastructure mapping for cyber.

title: What is Network Analysis?
section: What Network Analysis Can and Cannot Do
text:
What Network Analysis Can and Cannot Do

  
    What It Can Do
    
      Identify structurally important nodes independent of analyst preconception
      Detect communities and subgroups within large datasets
      Track network change over time — growth, contraction, reorganization
      Quantify network resilience and vulnerability
      Generate competing hypotheses about structure and function
      Integrate multiple data types (financial, communication, geospatial) into a unified model
      Prioritize collection gaps by identifying structurally important but poorly covered nodes
    
  
  
    What It Cannot Do
    
      Infer intent from structure alone
      Compensate for missing data — partial networks can produce misleading centrality scores
      Establish causation: correlation in network structure does not explain why a relationship exists
      Replace source validation: garbage in, garbage out
      Produce finished intelligence without analytical interpretation
      Resolve questions of identity or attribution without corroborating intelligence
    
  







WarningMethodological Warning



Network analysis is a tool, not a conclusion. Structural findings must be interpreted in context, caveated for data incompleteness, and integrated with all-source analysis before appearing in any intelligence product.16

title: What is Network Analysis?
section: Key Analytical Questions Networks Can Answer
text:
Key Analytical Questions Networks Can Answer
Network analysis organizes analytical questions into four categories. Each maps to specific methods and tools covered across this course.

  
    Structural Questions
    
      Who are the most influential or critical nodes? (centrality)
      Are there distinct subgroups or factions? (community detection)
      How connected is the network overall? (density, components)
      What is the shortest path between two actors? (geodesic distance)
      Does the network have a hierarchical or flat structure? (hierarchy index)
    
    Vulnerability Questions
    
      Which node or edge removal would maximally fragment the network?
      Are there single points of failure — articulation points, bridges?
      How does the network respond to disruption? (robustness simulation)
      Has the network adapted after a previous disruption?
    
  
  
    Relational Questions
    
      Who is the likely broker between otherwise disconnected groups?
      Which actors occupy structurally equivalent positions?
      Is there evidence of coordination or coincidence in timing of ties?
      Who has disproportionate access to information flow?
    
    Temporal Questions
    
      How has the network evolved over time?
      Is the network growing or contracting?
      Did a specific event trigger network restructuring?
      Are new nodes being recruited into the network?

title: What is Network Analysis?
section: Data Sources for Intelligence Network Analysis
text:
Data Sources for Intelligence Network Analysis
Network data quality is the single most important variable in structural analysis. All intelligence network data is, to some degree, incomplete — clandestine actors evade collection, sources have gaps, and the data that exists has varying reliability.

OSINT-Derived Network Data

Social media: follower/following graphs, interaction networks, co-hashtag networks
Corporate registries: beneficial ownership, director interlocks, subsidiary structures
Court records and indictments: named co-conspirators, financial transactions, documented meetings
News and event data: co-occurrence of actors in events, travel, public statements
Leaked databases: Panama Papers, FinCEN Files, Pandora Papers



Classified and Controlled Source Data

SIGINT: Communications metadata — who called whom, when, for how long, from where
HUMINT: Reported relationships, organizational rosters, physical meeting reports
Financial intelligence: Transaction records, account associations, correspondent banking relationships
Biometric and identity data: Co-location events, travel records, border crossings
Law enforcement databases: Known associates, gang rosters, watch lists







WarningData Quality and Completeness



All network data in intelligence contexts is incomplete. Clandestine actors evade collection. Analysts must reason carefully about what is missing and how gaps affect structural conclusions. A high-betweenness score may reflect genuine structural importance — or simply reflect the portion of the network that was collected.17

This course builds competency across three integrated dimensions:

Conceptual — Graph theory, centrality measures, community structure, temporal dynamics, multi-layer networks: the mathematical foundations that make quantitative analysis possible.

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Key Terms


Graph \(G = (V, E)\)

A set of nodes \(V\) and edges \(E \subseteq V \times V\).

Node (vertex)

An entity in the network — person, organization, location, event, account, or other discrete unit.

Edge (link, tie)

A relationship between two nodes; carries attributes including weight, direction, timestamp, and type.

Directed graph (digraph)

A graph in which edges have an explicit source and target; the relationship is asymmetric.

Weighted graph

A graph in which each edge carries a numeric value encoding relationship strength, frequency, or volume.

Bipartite graph

A graph with two distinct node types; edges run only between types, not within.

Density \(\Delta\)

The ratio of observed edges to the maximum possible edges; a global measure of network connectedness.

Dark network

A covert, trust-based relational system operating outside legal or institutional frameworks; characterized by deliberate sparsity and adaptive resilience.

title: What is Network Analysis?
text:
Key Takeaways

Network analysis is a relational paradigm — structure matters as much as (often more than) individual attributes.
The same mathematical framework applies across all domains: social, financial, infrastructure, information, global security.
Density, directionality, and edge weight fundamentally change what a network tells you and what metrics are appropriate.
Dark networks are deliberately sparse; bridge nodes with high betweenness centrality are the highest-value targets for disruption.
Network analysis has real, hard limits: incomplete data and structural findings always require interpretive judgment by a trained analyst.

section: CISA Critical Infrastructure Sectors and Network Taxonomy
text:
CISA Critical Infrastructure Sectors and Network Taxonomy
CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) designates 16 critical infrastructure sectors whose incapacity or destruction would have a debilitating effect on national security, public health, or economic security.1



16 CISA Sectors
Chemical · Commercial Facilities · Communications · Critical Manufacturing · Dams · Defense Industrial Base · Emergency Services · Energy · Financial Services · Food and Agriculture · Government Facilities · Healthcare and Public Health · Information Technology · Nuclear · Transportation Systems · Water and Wastewater


Network Modeling Priority
Not all sectors are equally amenable to network analysis. Sectors with well-defined physical nodes and edges are most directly modeled:

Directly modelable (physical network): Energy (power grids, pipelines), Transportation (aviation, maritime, rail, road), Communications (internet, undersea cables), Water (treatment plants and mains)
Indirectly modelable (institutional network): Financial Services (correspondent banking), Healthcare (hospital referral networks), Defense Industrial Base (supply chain network)



Shared Properties of Infrastructure Networks

Physical embedding: nodes and edges are constrained by geography; planar or near-planar topology limits maximum degree; betweenness is driven by geographic necessity rather than organizational design — chokepoints arise from terrain, not choice
Capacity constraints: edges have finite throughput (transmission capacity MW, lane capacity vehicles/hour, bandwidth Gbps); flow networks with capacity limits rather than simple binary-edge graphs
Redundancy by design: engineered infrastructure includes deliberate redundancy; this redundancy is often geographically uneven — dense in urban cores, thin in rural corridors
Interdependency: all 16 sectors are mutually dependent; failure in one cascades into others (Week 7 multilayer cascade models apply directly here)
Long asset lifetimes: infrastructure built decades ago was not designed for current threat models; older networks often have lower redundancy, simpler topology, and weaker cybersecurity









NoteThe Interdependency Graph as an Analytical Object



The 16 CISA sectors are themselves nodes in a sector-level interdependency network — a graph in which sectors are connected by dependency relationships. Edge \((A, B)\) indicates that sector \(A\) depends on sector \(B\): Energy depends on IT (for SCADA control), Transportation depends on Energy (for fuel and signals), Water depends on Energy (for pumping), and so on.
Community detection on this interdependency graph reveals tight dependency clusters: Energy-IT-Communications form the most densely interconnected cluster. A failure that propagates through this cluster has the widest cross-sector cascade footprint.
This is exactly the multilayer interdependency analysis introduced in Week 7 (Buldyrev et al. 2010) applied at the policy sector level rather than the individual node level.








WarningKey Distinction: Topology vs. Operations



Graph-theoretic vulnerability analysis identifies topological vulnerabilities — nodes and edges whose removal degrades network structure. This is distinct from operational vulnerability assessment, which accounts for protection levels, redundant systems, operator responses, and time-to-restore estimates.
Network analysis provides the structural foundation; operational context determines actionable priority. The two must be combined in any complete infrastructure vulnerability intelligence product.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
section: Error and Attack Tolerance: Random vs. Targeted Failure
text:
Error and Attack Tolerance: Random vs. Targeted Failure



Albert, Jeong, and Barabási (2000) — Nature
The foundational study of infrastructure network vulnerability demonstrated a fundamental asymmetry in how scale-free networks respond to two failure modes.2
Random Failure (Errors)
Nodes fail randomly with equal probability — equipment malfunction, natural disaster affecting random locations. Scale-free networks are highly robust to random failure: because most nodes are low-degree, random removal is unlikely to hit the rare high-degree hubs. The giant component remains intact through removal of up to ~80% of nodes. The power law degree distribution provides an extraordinary buffer against accidents.
Targeted Attack
Nodes are removed in decreasing order of degree or betweenness — an adversary who knows the network structure. Scale-free networks are catastrophically fragile to targeted attack: removing as few as 5–10% of nodes (the hubs) causes rapid collapse of the giant component and network fragmentation. Exponential (Erdős-Rényi) networks degrade similarly under targeted and random attacks — neither as robust nor as fragile as scale-free networks at the extremes.


The Achilles’ Heel
Albert et al. identified what they called the “Achilles’ heel” of scale-free networks: the same property — the presence of high-degree hubs — that makes them robust to accidents makes them uniquely vulnerable to deliberate attack by an adversary who knows the network topology.
Infrastructure design implication: most physical infrastructure networks (internet, aviation, power grids) were not designed to have scale-free topology; this property emerged from organic growth processes. The topology’s vulnerability to targeted attack was not a design choice — but it is a structural reality that adversaries can exploit.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
section: Percolation Theory and the Giant Component Threshold
text:
Percolation Theory and the Giant Component Threshold


Percolation theory studies the behavior of connected clusters as nodes or edges are randomly added to or removed from a network. Applied to infrastructure failure, it predicts when a network undergoes a percolation transition — a sudden collapse from a connected giant component to a fragmented set of small components.3
Bond percolation (edge failure): each edge fails independently with probability \(1 - p\). What fraction of edges must survive to maintain giant component connectivity?
Site percolation (node failure): each node fails independently with probability \(1 - p\). What fraction of nodes must survive?
Critical threshold \(p_c\) for random graphs \(G(n,p)\):
\[p_c = \frac{1}{\langle k \rangle}\]
Below \(p_c\): only small disconnected clusters remain. Above \(p_c\): a giant component spanning a finite fraction of nodes exists.
Scale-free networks (\(\gamma \leq 3\)): \(p_c \to 0\) for random failure. The network maintains a giant component for any finite fraction of surviving nodes — extraordinary robustness to accidents.
Targeted attack threshold (Cohen et al. 2001):4
\[p_c^{\text{targeted}} \approx \frac{1}{\kappa - 1} \quad \text{where} \quad \kappa = \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle}\]
For scale-free networks, \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) diverges with system size (due to hubs), making \(\kappa \gg 1\) and \(p_c^{\text{targeted}}\) extremely small. Only a tiny fraction of targeted hub removals is needed to collapse the network.

WarningInfrastructure Policy Implication



Critical infrastructure networks with scale-free degree distributions are extremely fragile to intentional targeted attack even though they are resilient to accidents. Security investment should be radically unequal — concentrated at high-degree and high-betweenness nodes, not distributed uniformly across the network.
Equal per-node security investment is the analytically wrong policy for a scale-free infrastructure. It provides near-uniform protection against the least likely failure mode (targeted removal of low-degree nodes) while under-protecting against the most likely adversary strategy (targeted removal of high-degree hubs).








NoteThe Percolation Transition is Discontinuous



For interdependent multilayer networks (Week 7, Buldyrev et al. 2010), the percolation transition changes character: it becomes first-order (abrupt, discontinuous) rather than the gradual second-order transition of single-layer networks. The system can appear stable until a sudden catastrophic collapse — with no early warning from gradual degradation signals. This makes monitoring interdependent infrastructure fundamentally harder than monitoring a single-layer network.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
section: Power Grid Structure and Small-World Properties
text:
Power Grid Structure and Small-World Properties



Power Grid as a Network

Nodes: generators (power plants), substations (voltage transformation and switching), transformers, and load centers (industrial consumers, distribution networks)
Edges: high-voltage transmission lines; weighted by voltage rating (kV) and power capacity (MW)
Directed or undirected? Power flows bidirectionally on AC lines in normal operation; edges are typically undirected in topology analysis, but directed in power flow (DC approximation) analysis
Power grids are near-planar (transmission lines generally cannot cross) but not perfectly planar (overhead lines in different layers may physically cross)
Average degree is low: \(\langle k \rangle \approx 2.7\) for the U.S. Western grid — highly sparse; average substation has only 2–3 connections



Small-World Properties
Power grids exhibit small-world properties: high clustering coefficient relative to a random graph with the same degree sequence, but relatively short average path length. This was demonstrated by Watts and Strogatz (1998) using the U.S. Western power grid as one of their three canonical examples:5

The high clustering relative to a random graph reflects the geographic clustering of generation and load: substations in the same region are highly interconnected; inter-regional connections are sparse.



Holmgren (2006): Swedish Grid Vulnerability
Äj Holmgren applied graph-theoretic vulnerability analysis to the Swedish transmission network:6

Average path length increased exponentially as high-betweenness substations were removed; degree-based targeting was significantly less effective — betweenness, not degree, is the correct targeting criterion for power grids
A small number of “super-substations” (high betweenness, moderate degree) were responsible for more than 60% of overall network connectivity; their removal fragmented the grid into isolated components
Redundancy was geographically uneven: urban core nodes had multiple alternative paths; rural transmission corridors were single-path with articulation points







WarningPower Flow vs. Graph-Theoretic Analysis



Graph-theoretic analysis (this course) identifies topological vulnerabilities — nodes and edges whose removal degrades connectivity structure. Full power engineering analysis uses power flow equations (AC or DC approximation) to model actual electrical physics: voltage stability, reactive power, frequency regulation, and generator dispatch.
The two approaches are complementary. Graph-theoretic analysis is faster, requires less data, and identifies structural vulnerabilities. Power flow analysis is required for operational assessment of specific failure scenarios. Intelligence products use the graph approach for priority ranking and the power flow approach (when operational data is available) for confirmation.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
text:
Cascading Failure: Mechanism and Modeling



The Cascade Mechanism
Cascading failures in power grids follow a specific sequence:7

Initial failure event removes one or more nodes or edges (equipment fault, extreme weather, deliberate attack, cyberattack on SCADA)
Load redistribution: load previously carried by the failed component is redistributed to surviving components according to the network’s flow dynamics
Overload cascade: components receiving excess redistributed load may exceed their capacity thresholds and fail in turn
Iterative cascade: each failure triggers another round of load redistribution; continues until the network reaches a new stable state or fully collapses
Cross-layer propagation: in interdependent infrastructure (grid × SCADA communications), cascade crosses system boundaries — power failure causes communication failures, which prevent operators from responding to the power failure



Motter-Lai Model (2002)
Each node \(i\) has capacity \(C_i = (1+\alpha)L_i^0\) where \(L_i^0\) is initial load (proportional to betweenness) and \(\alpha\) is the tolerance parameter — the fraction of excess capacity above the initial load. If \(\alpha\) is small, small perturbations trigger large cascades.
Cascade parameters:

Load proxy: betweenness centrality is used as a proxy for load (flows travel along shortest paths); in practice, power flow requires DC or AC power flow solvers
Redistribution rule: after a node fails, its load is distributed to neighboring nodes proportionally by their remaining capacity
Cascade termination: simulation ends when no further failures occur or the giant component collapses

Schneider et al. (2011) mitigation finding: Selectively increasing the capacity of high-betweenness nodes (rather than uniform capacity increases) provides the most cost-effective cascade resistance. A targeted 5% capacity increase at the top 10% of betweenness nodes reduced cascading loss by 25%.8

TipUkraine Power Grid Attacks 2015–2016



The December 2015 and December 2016 Ukrainian power grid attacks (attributed to Russia’s Sandworm/GRU) were the first confirmed cyberattacks to cause electric power outages to civilian populations.
2015 attack: Coordinated spear-phishing gained access to three regional distribution companies’ SCADA systems; operators remotely opened circuit breakers at 30 substations; ~230,000 customers lost power for 1–6 hours. Attackers also deployed BlackEnergy malware to overwrite firmware on serial-to-Ethernet converters — preventing remote restoration and requiring manual intervention at each substation.
Network analysis implication: the attackers did not need to identify the highest-betweenness substations to cause significant disruption. Targeting 30 mid-level distribution substations produced regional outages. The graph-theoretic model correctly predicts that betweenness-targeted attacks produce maximum fragmentation; but operational disruption (not maximum fragmentation) can be achieved with much lower-betweenness targeting in a distribution network where end-nodes (residential customers) have no redundancy.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
text:
Aviation: The Global Airport Network



World Airport Network (WAN)

Nodes: commercial airports (~3,880 worldwide with scheduled service)
Edges: direct scheduled flight routes; undirected (routes are bidirectional); weighted by weekly seat capacity or flight frequency
Highly scale-free: degree distribution follows a power law; a small number of major hub airports (Atlanta, Dubai, London Heathrow, Beijing, Chicago O’Hare) handle a disproportionate share of all connections
Small-world structure: average path length between any two airports is approximately 4.4 hops; most airports can reach any other airport within 2 connections via a major hub
Weighted strength centrality: for epidemiological and flow analysis, use strength (sum of edge weights = total seat capacity) rather than degree; airports with many low-frequency routes have different analytical significance than those with fewer high-frequency routes



Community Structure of the WAN
Community detection on the WAN produces geographically coherent communities: North American, European, East Asian, Middle Eastern, African, and Latin American clusters.
Inter-community bridge airports (Dubai DXB, London LHR, Singapore SIN, Istanbul IST) have extreme betweenness centrality — the structural chokepoints for global air travel. Disrupting Dubai or London Heathrow would fragment the global aviation network into largely disconnected regional clusters, consistent with scale-free network attack tolerance predictions.
COVID-19 natural experiment: The near-complete collapse of international routes in March–April 2020 produced an unplanned natural experiment. The WAN’s giant component collapsed rapidly under the equivalent of targeted hub removal — hub airports saw the largest traffic reductions first, consistent with scale-free attack predictions. Regional clusters became nearly isolated, reachable only through infrequent remaining inter-community edges.

TipIntelligence Application: Fugitive Travel Route Analysis



The scale-free hub structure of the WAN enables a specific intelligence analytical task: identifying evasive travel routes — paths from origin to destination that minimize exposure to major hub airports under allied jurisdiction (where law enforcement cooperation and biometric systems are most likely to intercept).
An adversary traveling from City A to City B while avoiding US, UK, EU, and Australian airports is constrained to routes through non-Western hubs. The network analysis task: compute all shortest paths between A and B; filter to paths that avoid designated jurisdiction airports; rank by number of hops and layover duration; identify which non-Western hub airports appear most frequently on feasible evasive routes — these are the airports most likely used for sensitive travel and the highest-priority collection points.
The scale-free WAN structure means few alternative paths exist when major Western hubs are removed — constraining evasive routes to a small number of non-allied hub airports (Dubai, Istanbul, Doha, Kuala Lumpur, Beijing).

Global Maritime Network

Nodes: ports, anchorages, and maritime waypoints
Edges: shipping routes derived from AIS (Automatic Identification System) vessel tracking data; weighted by vessel frequency and cargo tonnage
Chokepoints are geographic features (straits, canals) that appear as high-betweenness edges in the maritime spatial network; their closure forces cargo along dramatically longer alternative routes

Panama Canal 2023–24 drought: Reduced water levels in Gatún Lake forced the Panama Canal Authority to reduce daily transits from 36–38 to 18–22 vessels and impose draft restrictions. This effectively halved the canal’s throughput — a naturally-induced capacity constraint equivalent to partial bridge removal in a graph model. Container shipping costs on key Asia–East Coast routes increased 80%+ within 90 days, demonstrating the economic impact of even partial chokepoint disruption.



Undersea Cable Networks
Undersea fiber-optic cables carry approximately 95–99% of international internet traffic; satellite carries less than 5% and at higher latency.
Network structure:

Cable Landing Stations (CLS): fixed, physically located, publicly identified nodes. The CLS are the critical infrastructure — not the cables themselves, which are hardened and deep
Geographic concentration: CLS are geographically clustered (Egypt/Suez zone, Strait of Malacca, UK west coast, US East and West Coasts); a single extreme event at a cluster can disrupt multiple cables simultaneously
Articulation points: several single-CLS nodes in the cable network have no alternative routing — their failure permanently severs connectivity for the region they serve







WarningNord Stream and Red Sea Precedents



The September 2022 sabotage of Nord Stream 1 and 2 (attributed to state actors by EU investigations) demonstrated that undersea infrastructure — previously considered physically secure due to depth and remoteness — is a viable target for covert operations.
The February 2024 Houthi/Yemen-linked damage to three undersea cables in the Red Sea (Seacom, TGN-Eurasia/India, EIG cables) disrupted approximately 25% of internet traffic between Asia, Europe, and East Africa. Cable repair ships require months for deep-water repairs, and repair operations in contested maritime zones require naval escort. The Red Sea incidents represent the first documented case of conflict-zone undersea cable interdiction affecting global internet infrastructure.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
section: Internet Topology: Autonomous Systems and BGP
text:
Internet Topology: Autonomous Systems and BGP



The Internet as a Network of Networks

Nodes: Autonomous Systems (ASes) — independently administered routing domains, each with a unique AS number (ASN). Approximately 80,000 active globally.
Edges: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) peering relationships; an edge exists if two ASes exchange routing announcements; directionality reflects customer/provider vs. peer relationships
Scale-free topology: AS degree distribution follows a power law. A small number of Tier 1 carriers (AT&T, Lumen, NTT, Telia, Cogent) have global reach and peer with all others; most ASes are stub networks (leaf nodes) attached to one or a few providers

Internet Exchange Points (IXPs): Physical facilities where multiple ASes interconnect and exchange traffic; operated by neutral third parties. High-traffic IXPs (AMS-IX Amsterdam, DE-CIX Frankfurt, LINX London, Equinix NY, MSK-IX Moscow) are the internet’s most critical betweenness nodes. Disrupting a major IXP would affect internet connectivity for an entire region.


BGP as an Attack Surface
BGP was designed for trust between network operators — it has no cryptographic authentication of route origin. BGP route hijacking: an AS announces routes for IP prefixes it does not legitimately own; other ASes may prefer the hijacked route and direct traffic through the attacker’s infrastructure.
This is a graph-level attack: a node claims control of edges it does not own; the attack succeeds when other nodes update their routing tables to prefer the false claim — a vote-based manipulation of the network’s routing state.
High-profile incidents:

Pakistan Telecom 2008: accidentally announced routes for YouTube’s IP prefixes; global YouTube outage for ~2 hours as traffic routed to Pakistan and dropped
Rostelecom 2020: announced routes for Amazon, Google, and major financial institutions’ prefixes; traffic briefly redirected through Russia — affecting financial system communications

NoteRPKI: Structural Mitigation for BGP Hijacking



Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is the cryptographic framework that allows IP address holders to create Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) — signed certificates stating which ASes are authorized to announce specific prefixes.
Network analysis of RPKI adoption shows it as a network property, not a node property: the effectiveness of RPKI depends on the fraction of AS paths that include at least one RPKI-validating router. An AS that validates RPKI but receives routing announcements from non-validating peers is not protected. This is a network percolation problem: RPKI provides protection only when the network has enough adopting nodes to constitute a connected validation path from source to destination.
As of 2025, approximately 40% of global BGP routes have valid RPKI certificates — sufficient for meaningful protection on major transit paths but inadequate for comprehensive protection of edge networks.

title: Infrastructure and Physical Networks
text:
Critical Node Identification: Four Methods



Beyond Single-Metric Ranking
Identifying critical nodes in infrastructure networks requires multiple complementary methods. The most important node depends on the adversary’s goal and the failure scenario being modeled.
Method 1: Betweenness Centrality
Identifies nodes controlling the most shortest paths; most relevant for flow disruption. Appropriate when: the adversary’s goal is to disrupt commodity flow through the network and the network operates on shortest-path routing. Limitation: does not account for capacity or flow redistribution; may underestimate articulation point importance in sparse grids where betweenness is distributed.
Method 2: Articulation Point Analysis
Identifies nodes whose removal disconnects the graph — absolute fragmentation, not just path lengthening. Computable in linear time \(O(V + E)\) via depth-first search. Appropriate when: the adversary’s goal is complete disconnection of network segments; physical infrastructure where alternative paths do not exist.
Method 3: Targeted Attack Simulation
Sequentially remove nodes by a selected criterion (degree, betweenness, or iterative betweenness recomputed after each removal); measure giant component size after each step. Produces a vulnerability curve: plots giant component fraction \(S\) vs. fraction of nodes removed \(f\); steeper drop = more fragile. The area under the vulnerability curve is a scalar resilience index: smaller area = more fragile.
Method 4: Network Efficiency Loss
\[\Delta E(v) = \frac{E(G) - E(G \setminus v)}{E(G)} \quad \text{where} \quad E(G) = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d_{ij}}\]
Rank nodes by the efficiency loss their removal causes. Captures both fragmentation and path lengthening effects simultaneously — more complete than betweenness alone.
